title: Assent may be firm yet groundless; true certainty needs a legitimate foundation in the thing
source_text: II. Porro ista assensus firmitas quandoque nullum habet in re ipsa fundamentum; sed oritur solum ab assentientis errore, affectu, vel pertinacia, & tum non est veri nominis certitudo. Qui enim certo credunt quae falsa sunt, non tam certi, quam persuasi dici debent. Alias vero firmus ejusmodi assensus clara perceptione, aut solida ratione, vel legitimo aliquo testimonio nititur. Et tum demum vera est, & proprie dicta certitudo: quae locum non habet, nisi ubi persuasio, non modo firma, sed vera atque legitima est. In praesenti vero quaestione ratio non habetur certitudinis illius prioris, & improprie dictae; sed posterioris solum certitudinis, quae non tantum notat firmitatem assensus in credente, vel cognoscente; sed etiam legitimum ejus, ex parte rei, fundamentum.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover that firmness of assent sometimes has no foundation in the thing itself, but arises only from the error, affection, or obstinacy of the one assenting, and then it is not certainty of the true name. For those who certainly believe what is false ought to be called not so much certain as persuaded. But at other times firm assent of this sort rests on clear perception, or solid reason, or some legitimate testimony. And then at last it is true and properly so-called certainty: which has place only where the persuasion is not only firm but also true and legitimate. But in the present question account is not taken of that former and improperly so-called certainty, but only of the latter certainty, which marks not only firmness of assent in the believer or knower, but also its legitimate foundation on the side of the thing.
pass_b_english: Firm assent without a real foundation is persuasion, not true certainty.
This controversy concerns only certainty that is both firm and legitimately grounded in the thing.
